records.postTitle:
Your doctor spent more than a decade in medical school and training. 

The person reviewing and denying the claim often has a few weeks of insurance-company training.

One of them decides what treatment you actually need. The other decides whether the insurance company will pay for it. 

That imbalance is baked into the system, and it is one of the reasons so many people feel the American healthcare setup stops making sense the moment a real bill shows up.

UnitedHealth Group reported roughly $5.5 billion in net income last quarter. 

At the same time, a KFF analysis of 2025 data found the company denied about 17% of standard prior-authorization requests in its Medicare Advantage plans — roughly 1 in 6

Patients pay premiums every single month, yet the insurer still decides whether many treatments, tests, or procedures get approved through the prior-authorization process. 

The contrast between the profit number and the denial rate is hard to ignore. 

It captures one of the central frustrations of American healthcare: you pay in, but coverage is never fully guaranteed until someone else signs off.
